picked.t: Vietnam set to overtake Southeast Asia's largest economy in GDP per capita this year
picked.body: The figures, from the IMF's October World Economic Outlook, put Vietnam's nominal output per person 8.9% above last year's level and nearly double what it was a decade earlier. Vietnam trailed Indonesia by about $250 last year, IMF estimates show, and the fund's April outlook had still projected Indonesia staying ahead in 2026. The new projections would make Vietnam fifth among ASEAN members, behind Singapore, Brunei, Malaysia and Thailand. The IMF expects it to keep its lead over Indonesia in 2027, at $5,659 against $5,550. Indonesia remains Southeast Asia's largest economy by far. With nearly three times Vietnam's population of just over 100 million, its GDP is projected at $1.48 trillion this year, against Vietnam's $542 billion. Nikkei Asia linked the shift to Vietnam's growing role in high-tech manufacturing of semiconductors and electronics, noting that Taiwan's Foxconn is expanding production there. South Korea's Samsung Electronics makes smartphones and other electronics for export at its northern Vietnamese factories. Vietnam's economy grew 9.95% in the third quarter, its fastest pace in four years. The government's public investment push is also supporting growth, Mai Fujita, a senior research fellow at Japan's Institute of Developing Economies, told Nikkei Asia . Vietnam plans to spend VND1.014 quadrillion ($39.3 billion) on public investment this year, with roads, airports and other infrastructure under construction nationwide. Indonesia's growth, by contrast, has hovered around 5%. The IMF forecasts 5.1% for the country this year, against 8.4% for Vietnam. Vietnam is targeting growth of at least 10% this year and aims to lift GDP per capita to about $8,500 by 2030, roughly Thailand's level today. Fujita said Vietnam also needs to pursue long-term growth by developing human resources and technology, alongside the infrastructure spending that lifts growth in the short term.

picked.t: [베트남 경제동향] 올해 1인당 GDP 인도네시아 추월 전망...동남아 경제 판도 변화
picked.body: 베트남의 산업단지에서 전자제품 및 제조업 생산이 진행되고 있다. 첨단 제조업 육성과 외국인 투자 확대는 베트남 경제성장의 주요 동력으로 꼽힌다. (사진=베트남 연합뉴스통신) (호치민=베트남코리아타임즈) 반 린 (Van Linh) 기자 = 베트남의 1인당 국내총생산(GDP)이 올해 인도네시아를 넘어설 것으로 전망됐다. 베트남이 그동안 인도네시아에 뒤처졌던 1인당 GDP에서 역전에 성공할 것으로 예상되면서 동남아시아 주요 경제국 간 경제구도에도 변화가 나타날 전망이다. 국제통화기금(IMF)이 지난 10월 발표한 세계경제전망(WEO)에 따르면 베트남의 올해 명목 1인당 GDP는 5,259달러로 예상됐다. 이는 지난해보다 8.9% 증가한 수준으로, 인도네시아의 예상치인 5,153달러를 106달러 웃도는 규모다. 베트남의 1인당 GDP는 2025년 4,829달러로 인도네시아의 5,078달러보다 낮았다. 그러나 올해 베트남 경제가 상대적으로 빠른 성장세를 보이면서 양국 간 순위가 뒤바뀔 것으로 전망됐다. 이번 전망이 현실화하면 베트남은 싱가포르, 브루나이, 말레이시아, 태국에 이어 아세안(ASEAN) 회원국 가운데 1인당 GDP 5위에 오르게 된다. IMF는 베트남의 1인당 GDP가 2027년 5,659달러로 상승해 인도네시아의 5,550달러를 계속 웃돌 것으로 예상했다. 다만 전체 경제 규모에서는 인도네시아가 여전히 베트남을 크게 앞서고 있다. 인도네시아의 올해 명목 GDP는 1조4,800억달러로 예상되는 반면 베트남은 5,420억달러 수준에 그칠 전망이다. 인도네시아의 인구가 약 2억9,000만명으로 베트남의 1억명보다 훨씬 많기 때문이다.   첨단 제조업과 인프라 투자가 성장 견인 베트남의 1인당 GDP 상승에는 제조업 고도화와 외국인 투자 확대, 정부의 적극적인 공공투자 등이 영향을 미친 것으로 분석된다. 특히 반도체와 전자제품 등 첨단 제조업 분야에서 베트남의 역할이 확대되고 있다. 대만 폭스콘(Foxconn)이 베트남 내 생산시설을 확대하고 있으며, 한국 삼성전자도 북부 지역 공장을 중심으로 스마트폰과 전자제품을 생산해 세계 시장에 공급하고 있다. 정부의 대규모 인프라 투자 역시 경제성장을 뒷받침하고 있다. 베트남은 올해 도로와 공항 등 국가 기반시설 확충을 위해 1,014조동(약 393억달러)을 공공투자에 투입할 계획이다. 전국적으로 고속도로와 공항 등 대형 인프라 사업이 진행되면서 건설 및 관련 산업의 성장에도 기여하고 있다. 경제성장률에서도 양국 간 차이가 두드러진다. IMF는 올해 베트남의 경제성장률을 8.4%로 전망한 반면 인도네시아는 5.1%로 예상했다. 베트남은 올해 3분기 국내총생산(GDP)이 전년 동기 대비 9.95% 증가해 최근 4년 사이 가장 높은 분기 성장률을 기록했다. 베트남 정부는 올해 경제성장률 목표를 최소 10%로 설정하고 있으며, 2030년까지 1인당 GDP를 약 8,500달러로 끌어올린다는 목표도 제시했다. 다만 1인당 GDP 순위 역전이 곧바로 국민의 실질적인 생활수준 역전을 의미하는 것은 아니다. 이번 전망은 물가 변동을 조정하지 않은 명목 GDP를 기준으로 하며, 달러 환산 과정에서 환율 변동도 영향을 미친다. 베트남이 향후 지속적인 성장세를 유지하기 위해서는 인프라 확충과 외국인 투자 유치뿐 아니라 노동생산성 향상, 기술 개발, 고급 인력 양성 등 산업 경쟁력을 높이기 위한 과제도 해결해야 한다. 베트남이 첨단 제조업 육성과 산업구조 고도화를 통해 동남아시아 주요 경제국으로서 입지를 얼마나 확대할 수 있을지 주목된다.   <저작권자(c) 베트남코리아타임즈, 무단 전재-재배포 금지>

picked.t: Moroccan student's journey from knowing only the local words for 'hello' to becoming Vietnam's top maritime navigation graduate
picked.body: A photograph of 23-year-old Moroccan student Hiba Faradji beaming as she accepted a top graduate award at Vietnam Maritime University in August quickly went viral across social media. However, behind this picture-perfect moment of triumph lies a deeply turbulent and emotionally taxing journey that nearly derailed her academic dreams. Her story began at the age of 18, when Faradji left her coastal hometown of Tangier, Morocco. Armed with a prestigious medical scholarship, she relocated to France to begin her studies at the renowned Sorbonne University in Paris. Unfortunately, her arrival coincided with the sudden, global outbreak of the Covid-19 pandemic. The unprecedented health crisis immediately threw her academic plans into chaos. Her coursework became increasingly difficult to manage, and her living situation grew highly unstable. Forced to repeatedly stay with acquaintances far from the university campus, Faradji simultaneously battled a series of personal setbacks. After enduring eight months of stress and isolation, the overwhelmed student made the difficult decision to abandon her medical studies entirely and return to Morocco, facing a highly uncertain future. Deeply discouraged by the setback, Faradji isolated herself at home for nearly seven months. The once-outgoing student found herself battling depression, withdrawing completely from the outside world and plagued by a constant fear of being controlled by others. As her mental health gradually stabilized, she resumed her search for international education programs. However, she quickly faced a new wave of obstacles, enduring repeated rejections from universities in both Spain and South Korea. In late 2022, just as she was feeling entirely out of options, a lifeline emerged. Faradji stumbled upon an announcement for four full academic scholarships being offered by the Vietnam Maritime University. Seeking a way out of her predicament, she applied for the university’s bachelor’s program in maritime navigation, encouraged by the full scholarship. Her family supported the decision, and a close friend of her mother even helped pay for her plane ticket. "I had very little time to prepare or learn about Vietnam. I just thought Hai Phong might be similar to my hometown, a coastal city that was neither too big nor too remote," Faradji recalled. Her first day in Vietnam was yet another memorable experience. In February 2023, Faradji arrived at Hanoi's Noi Bai International Airport just before the Lunar New Year, Vietnam's largest national holiday and the most important occasion for family reunion. With passenger buses practically unavailable during the peak travel season, she had little choice but to spend VND2.5 million (US$97), half the total cash she was carrying along at that moment, on a direct taxi to Hai Phong. She arrived to find her cold dormitory completely deserted, as local students had already left for their hometowns for the holiday, leaving her on the verge of tears and wishing she could fly straight back home. As her parents called to check on her, Faradji pulled herself together and told herself she had to keep going. Challenges continued Although she had a strong command of English and French, Faradji found her coursework "quite difficult" because of the specialized terminology and calculations involved. "Math has never been my strength, while Ship Stability is highly detailed and technical. It was so difficult that I could not cover the entire curriculum in just two semesters," she said. To overcome difficulties, she spent considerable time studying independently at home to keep up. She identified her biggest challenges as the psychological wounds she had carried from Paris, differences in daily life in a new environment, and being one of the few female students in a predominantly male department. As a Muslim, Faradji strictly avoids pork. During her first three months in Hai Phong, before becoming accustomed to local cuisine, she subsisted largely on nuts and dried foods sent by her mother. Poor nutrition caused her to lose 4 kg and suffer from prolonged insomnia. Language was another obstacle. Initially, she knew only one Vietnamese phrase: "xin chao," meaning "hello." After five months of basic Vietnamese lessons, combined with observing and imitating the people around her, she gradually became more confident. A turning point came when Faradji joined an English club, where she befriended a student named Thuy, who invited her to stay with her family. This gave Faradji an opportunity to practice speaking Vietnamese in everyday situations. She eventually became familiar even with distinctive expressions and speech patterns used by people in Hai Phong. Once she settled into her studies, Faradji began supporting herself by taking part-time jobs and renting her own apartment.
